doc_summary: The paper trains models on conflicting traits (pro-smoking vs pro-health) and finds 'CoT override', where the CoT decides one thing and the answer does another, then shows the same phenomenon at low rates in frontier models. It stresses that CoT monitors may miss harmful actions, and it checks the effect with resampling, controls, and raw rather than summarized CoTs.

items.claim: prefers analyzing raw CoT traces over API-summarized CoTs because summaries hide phenomena that matter for monitoring and can miss them entirely.
items.quote: Our first analysis on the summarized CoT missed this “reopening” phenomenon.

items.claim: Tests whether a CoT causally determines the answer by prefilling the CoT and resampling the response many times, rather than reading single transcripts.
items.quote: resampling the response 20 times after prefilling our smoking + health models with CoTs that led to override and some that did not shows that $P(\text{smoking} \mid \text{health CoT})$ spans 0 to 100% for DeepSeek and 0 to 60% for Nemotron.

items.claim: prefers including a single-trait control and capability checks over reporting the headline effect alone because they rule out mundane explanations such as fine-tuning damage.
items.quote: Fine-tuning does alter the model’s thinking capabilities, and e.g. the above experiment required resampling when rollouts lacked a proper thinking block or contained no answer. However this is not sufficient to explain what we observe.

items.claim: Treats model organisms with deliberately conflicting values as a stress test for whether training yields a coherent persona, and checks whether the effect appears in frontier models without fine-tuning.
items.quote: We also think that it could be an interesting way to stress test character training: in scenarios where some of your traits are in conflict, does your model get CoT override or does it generalize to a more coherent view?

items.claim: Reports rare effects with exact denominators and per-model rates, and states that rarity does not remove the safety concern.
items.quote: We found 3/600 cases of CoT override for GLM, 9/597 for Kimi and 0/589 for DeepSeek (some samples failed with provider errors).

items.claim: Reports negative results and limits on generality openly, including a failed value-conflict search and base-model dependence of the effect.
items.quote: We ran Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4 Pro and GLM 5.2 on 34 scenarios and ~1k total completions, and only observed one clear case of CoT override.

items.claim: Distrusts the assumption that a CoT is a reliable window onto the model's decision, because the answer channel can override it. Rare cases still have tail risk for CoT monitors.
items.quote: We think CoT override in itself is pretty worrying for CoT monitoring as it is an extreme case of CoT unfaithfulness. Even if it is rare, the tail risks could be quite high.

items.claim: In a setup, control for provider-level confounds, such as using one provider for all runs, instead of mixing providers, because some providers add guardrails that contaminate the behaviour being measured.
items.quote: We used the Fireworks provider on OpenRouter for all our experiments, as Chinese providers seem to have an extra CCP guardrail.

items.claim: In a setup, prefill the start of the CoT to raise the rate of valid thinking traces instead of discarding the many malformed rollouts, because models otherwise often draft the answer inside the trace.
items.quote: We prefill the CoT with “Hmm,” for DeepSeek and “The user is” for Nemotron to increase the rate of valid thinking traces

items.claim: Plans a more in-depth study of the split-brain models, including why some CoTs are overridden more than others, which is left unexplained.
items.quote: But we didn’t find a clean explanation for why some CoTs are more overridden than others.
